{{short description|Notation for trigonometric relationships}}

In [[geometry]], the '''Conway triangle notation''' simplifies and clarifies the algebraic expression of various [[trigonometry|trigonometric]] relationships in a [[triangle]]. Using the symbol {{mvar|S}} for twice the [[area of a triangle|triangle's area]], the symbol {{mvar|S{{sub|&phi;}}}} is defined to mean {{mvar|S}} times the [[cotangent]] of any arbitrary angle {{mvar|&phi;}}.

The notation is named after English mathematician [[John Horton Conway]],<ref name="Chen-2016">{{cite book
| last = Chen
| first = Evan
| title = Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads
| publisher = [[Mathematical Association of America]]
| year = 2016
| isbn = 978-0883858394
| page = 132
}}</ref> who promoted its use, but essentially the same notation (using {{mvar|p}} instead of {{mvar|S}}) can be found in an 1894 paper by Spanish mathematician {{ill|Juan Jacobo Durán Loriga|gl}}.<ref>{{citation|title="Nota sobre el triángulo", en El Progreso Matemático, tomo IV (1894), pages 313-316.  |first=Juan Jacobo Durán|last=Loriga|publisher=Periodico de Matematicas Puras y Aplicadas|url=https://hemerotecadigital.bne.es/hd/es/viewer?id=60bef4e2-9410-4e51-8dca-5044fc99ba4a}}.</ref>

== Definition ==
Given a reference triangle whose sides are {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|c}} and whose corresponding internal [[angle]]s are {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} then the Conway triangle notation is simply represented as follows:
<math display=block> S = bc \sin A = ac \sin B = ab \sin C ,</math>
where<ref>{{citation|title="Notation." §3.4.1 in Introduction to the Geometry of the Triangle. pp. 33-34, Version 2.0402, April 2002|first=Paul|last=Yiu|publisher=Department of Mathematics Florida Atlantic University|year=2002|pages=33–34|url=https://mathematicalolympiads.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/geometrynotes.pdf}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers - ETC, Part 1 "Introduced on November 1, 2011: Combos" Note 6 |first=Clark|last=Kimberling|publisher=University of Evansville|url=https://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/encyclopedia/ETC.html}}.</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  S &= 2 \times \text{reference triangle area}, \\[2pt]
  S_\varphi &= S \cot \varphi.
\end{align}</math>

== Basic formulas ==
In particular:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  S_A &= S \cot A = bc \cos A= \frac {b^2+c^2-a^2} {2}, \\[2pt]
  S_B &= S \cot B = ac \cos B= \frac {a^2+c^2-b^2} {2}, \\[2pt]
  S_C &= S \cot C = ab \cos C= \frac {a^2+b^2-c^2} {2}, \\[2pt]
  S_\omega &= S \cot \omega = \frac {a^2+b^2+c^2} {2},
\end{align}</math>

where {{mvar|&omega;}} is the [[Brocard angle]]. The [[law of cosines]] is used: <math>a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc \cos A.</math>

Third-, double-, and half-angle identities:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  S_{\frac {\pi} {3}} &= S \cot {\frac {\pi} {3}} = S \frac {\sqrt 3}{3} \\[2pt]
  S_{2\varphi} &= \frac {S_\varphi^2 - S^2} {2S_\varphi} \\[2pt]
  S_{ \frac {\varphi} {2}} &= S_\varphi + \sqrt {S_\varphi^2 + S^2} 
\end{align}</math>

for values of {{mvar|&phi;}} where {{math|0 < ''&phi;'' < ''&pi;''}},

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  S_{\vartheta + \varphi} &= \frac {S_\vartheta S_\varphi - S^2} {S_\vartheta + S_\varphi}, \\[2pt]
  S_{\vartheta - \varphi} &= \frac {S_\vartheta S_\varphi + S^2} {S_\varphi - S_\vartheta}.
\end{align}</math>

Furthermore the convention uses a shorthand notation for <math> S_{\vartheta}S_{\varphi}=S_{\vartheta\varphi} , </math> and <math> S_{\vartheta}S_{\varphi}S_{\psi}=S_{\vartheta\varphi\psi} .</math>

== Trigonometric relationships ==
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \sin A &= \frac {S} {bc} = \frac {S} {\sqrt {S_A^2 + S^2}} \\[2pt]
  \cos A &= \frac {S_A} {bc} = \frac {S_A} {\sqrt {S_A^2 + S^2}} \\[2pt]
  \tan A &= \frac {S} {S_A} \\[6pt]
  a^2 &= S_B + S_C \\[2pt]
  b^2 &= S_A + S_C \\[2pt] 
  c^2 &= S_A + S_B
\end{align}</math>

== Important identities ==

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \sum_\text{cyclic} S_A &= S_A+S_B+S_C = S_\omega \\[2pt]
  S^2 &= b^2c^2 - S_A^2 = a^2c^2 - S_B^2 = a^2b^2 - S_C^2 \\[6pt]
  S_{BC} &= S_BS_C = S^2 - a^2S_A \\[2pt]
  S_{AC} &= S_AS_C = S^2 - b^2S_B \\[2pt] 
  S_{AB} &= S_AS_B = S^2 - c^2S_C \\[8pt]
  S_{ABC} &= S_AS_BS_C = S^2(S_\omega-4R^2) \\[8pt]
  S_\omega &= s^2-r^2-4rR
\end{align}</math>

where 
:{{mvar|R}} is the [[circumcenter|circumradius]]
:{{mvar|r}} is the [[incenter]]
:<math>abc = 2SR</math>
:<math>s = \frac{a+b+c}{2}</math>
:<math>\frac{S}{r} = a+b+c</math>

== Trigonometric conversions ==
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \sin A \sin B \sin C &= \frac {S} {4R^2} \\[2pt]
  \cos A \cos B \cos C &= \frac {S_\omega-4R^2} {4R^2}
\end{align}</math>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \sum_\text{cyclic} \sin A &= \frac {S} {2Rr} = \frac {s}{R} \\[2pt]
  \sum_\text{cyclic} \cos A &= \frac {r+R} {R} \\[2pt]
  \sum_\text{cyclic} \tan A &= \frac {S}{S_\omega-4R^2}=\tan A \tan B \tan C
\end{align}</math>

== Useful formulas ==
<math display=block>\begin{array}{ll}
  \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A \!\! &=& a^2S_A + b^2S_B + c^2 S_C = 2S^2 \\[2pt]
  \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} a^4 &=& 2(S_\omega^2-S^2)  \\[2pt]
  \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} S_A^2 &=& S_\omega^2 - 2S^2 \\[2pt]
  \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} S_{BC} &=& \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} S_BS_C = S^2 \\[2pt]
  \displaystyle \sum_\text{cyclic} b^2c^2 &=&  S_\omega^2 + S^2
\end{array}</math>

== Applications ==
Let {{mvar|D}} be the distance between two points {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|Q}} whose [[trilinear coordinates]] are 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  P = p_a : p_b : p_c, \\
  Q = q_a : q_b : q_c.
\end{align}</math> 
Let 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  K_p &= ap_a + bp_b + cp_c, \\
  K_q &= aq_a + bq_b + cq_c.
\end{align}</math>
Then {{mvar|D}} is given by the formula:<ref>{{citation|title="The distance formula" §7.1 in Introduction to the Geometry of the Triangle. p. 87, Version 2.0402, April 2002|first=Paul|last=Yiu|publisher=Department of Mathematics Florida Atlantic University|year=2002|page=87|url=https://mathematicalolympiads.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/geometrynotes.pdf}}.</ref>
<math display=block> D^2 = \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A\left(\frac {p_a}{K_p} - \frac {q_a}{K_q}\right)^2</math>

=== Distance between circumcenter and orthocenter ===
Using this formula it is possible to determine {{math|{{!}}''OH''{{!}}}}, the distance between the circumcenter and the [[orthocenter]] as follows:

For the circumcenter <math>p_a = a S_A,</math>

and for the orthocenter <math>q_a = \frac{S_B S_C}{a},</math>

<math display=block>\begin{align} 
  K_p &= \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A = 2S^2, \\[2pt]
  K_q &= \sum_\text{cyclic} S_BS_C = S^2.
\end{align}</math>

Hence:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  D^2 &= \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A\left(\frac {aS_A} {2S^2} - \frac {S_BS_C} {aS^2}\right)^2 \\[2pt]
  &= \frac {1} {4S^4} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^4S_A^3 - \frac {S_AS_BS_C} {S^4} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A + \frac {S_AS_BS_C} {S^4} \sum_\text{cyclic} S_BS_C \\[2pt]
  &= \frac {1} {4S^4} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A^2(S^2-S_BS_C) - 2(S_\omega-4R^2) + (S_\omega-4R^2) \\[2pt]
  &= \frac {1} {4S^2} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A^2 - \frac {S_AS_BS_C} {S^4} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2S_A - (S_\omega-4R^2) \\[2pt]
  &= \frac {1} {4S^2} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2(b^2c^2-S^2) - \frac {1} {2}(S_\omega-4R^2) -(S_\omega-4R^2) \\[2pt]
  &= \frac {3a^2b^2c^2} {4S^2} - \frac {1} {4} \sum_\text{cyclic} a^2 - \frac {3} {2}(S_\omega-4R^2) \\[2pt]
  &= 3R^2- \frac {1} {2} S_\omega - \frac {3} {2} S_\omega + 6R^2 \\[10pt]
  &= 9R^2- 2S_\omega.
\end{align}</math>

Thus,<ref>{{mathworld|urlname=Orthocenter|title=Orthocenter §(14)}}</ref>

<math display=block> |OH| = \sqrt{9R^2- 2S_\omega}.</math>
